newsitem.title: JAPAN: NTT says hopes to launch int'l service by end '97.
newsitem.headline: NTT says hopes to launch int'l service by end '97.

text.p: Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp said on Wednesday that it hopes to start providing international telephone services to multinational companies in Europe, the United States and Asia by the end of this year.
NTT president Junichiro Miyazu told a news conference that the company would apply on Wednesday for communications business licences in Britain, Germany and France.
NTT added it hopes to apply soon for similar licences in the United States and Asia.

Under a service to be called NTT Global Service, the company plans to offer sophisticated communications services, such as frame relay services, by connecting multinationals located in Britain, Germany, France and the United States.
NTT for the time being will not directly handle communications between Japan and those countries.
Miyazu said NTT hoped to offer such services from Japan as soon as a law on breaking up NTT passes parliament.
The law will be discussed in a parliamentary session which starts later this month.
When the law is revised, NTT hopes to provide broader and more comprehensive services, Miyazu said. The services would be targetted at individual and corporate users.
He added that alliances, investments in and mergers with international telecommunications operators were possible as NTT develops its international services.

Using NTT's proposed service, multinational conglomerates will be able to send voice and data messages along international telephone lines to their group companies in Europe, the United States and Asia.
NTT would not be able to include Japan in the loop until the law on its status was revised in the middle of this year, but the time lag should be short, it said.
NTT will lease lines from other companies to provide the service in the initial stages, but said it may lay its own fixed lines in due course.
An NTT spokesman said NTT would also help Japanese multinationals in the targeted regions to construct in-house computer networks.
NTT has already assigned 50 NTT workers to help build such corporate networks and extend them internationally in 13 cities in Europe, the Unites States and Asia, the spokesman said.
The NTT spokesman said profits would be small at first because of tough competition in this kind of specialist market. He did not give any specific estimates for sales or investment.

NTT has long sought to break into the lucrative international market but its entry has been delayed by wrangling between NTT managers and the government over whether the giant company should be broken up into smaller entities.

Under a compromise deal announced in early December, the giant NTT will be broken up into a set of companies under the wing of a holding company. One of the companies will be allowed to offer international services.
